modules.title: Module 1 - AI and machine learning fundamentals

lessons.title: AI, machine learning and deep learning

blocks.value:
## Three terms that nest together
The AIF-C01 exam starts by demanding clarity about three words many people use as synonyms, but which form a nesting relationship.

**Artificial intelligence (AI)** is the broadest field: any technique that makes a computer imitate capabilities associated with human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing images, or making decisions. A system of hand-written rules can already be considered AI.

**Machine learning (ML)** is a subset of AI in which the system learns patterns from data, instead of just following fixed rules. You do not program the answer; you show examples and the algorithm figures out the rule.

**Deep learning** is a subset of ML based on neural networks with many layers. It is what powers recent advances in vision, language, and generative AI.
The hierarchy lands right on the exam: AI contains machine learning, which in turn contains deep learning.

## Why the distinction matters
Knowing what contains what avoids the exam's most common traps, like "deep learning encompasses AI" (false) or "AI is a special case of ML" (false). The path always goes from the most general to the most specific: AI, then ML, then deep learning.

In practice, when a scenario talks about learning from data, you are in machine learning territory. When it specifically mentions deep neural networks for image, sound, or free text, it is deep learning.

questions.statement: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning?
options: ML is a subset of AI, and deep learning is a subset of ML
Deep learning contains machine learning, which contains AI
Machine learning is broader than artificial intelligence
AI and machine learning are separate areas, with no overlap

questions.statement: A system learns to identify cats in photos from thousands of labeled examples, with no hand-written rules. This system is best described as:
options: A spreadsheet with deterministic formulas
A relational database queried by SQL
A system of fixed rules manually written by people
Machine learning, because it learns patterns from data

questions.statement: Deep learning stands apart from other machine learning techniques mainly by:
options: Being unable to handle images, audio, or free text
Using neural networks with many layers to learn complex patterns
Dispensing with any kind of training data entirely
Working only with logic rules hand-written by experts

questions.statement: A vendor presents a decision system built only with hand-written rules, learning nothing from data. About classifying this system, what is correct?
options: It is not AI, because AI requires learning from data
It is deep learning, because it organizes rules in layers
It is machine learning, because it makes automated decisions
It can be considered AI, but not machine learning

questions.statement: Which sentence below contains a conceptual ERROR according to the hierarchy between AI, machine learning, and deep learning?
options: Every AI system learns patterns from data
Every deep learning system is also machine learning
Every machine learning system is also AI
There is machine learning that does not use deep neural networks

lessons.title: Types of learning: supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement

blocks.value:
## Three ways to learn
Machine learning organizes into families, and the AIF-C01 expects you to recognize which one applies to a scenario.

**Supervised learning** trains with data that already has the right answer (the label). The model learns to map inputs to known outputs. Example: predicting whether an email is spam using thousands of emails already marked as spam or not.

**Unsupervised learning** works with unlabeled data and looks for hidden structure, like grouping similar items. Example: segmenting customers into behavior groups with no predefined categories.

**Reinforcement learning** learns by trial and error: an agent takes actions, receives rewards or penalties, and adjusts its strategy to maximize reward over time. Example: a system that learns to play a game or control a robot.

[["Type","Uses labels?","What it seeks","Example"],["Supervised","Yes","Predict a known output","Detect fraud with labeled transactions"],["Unsupervised","No","Find groups or patterns","Segment customers by behavior"],["Reinforcement","No (uses rewards)","Maximize reward by trial and error","Control a robot or play a game"]]

## How to decide in the scenario
Look for the keyword. If the statement mentions already-labeled data or a known right answer, it is supervised. If it talks about discovering groups or patterns with no ready categories, it is unsupervised. If it describes an agent that acts, receives rewards, and improves over time, it is reinforcement.

questions.statement: A carrier wants to predict customer churn using a history where each customer is already marked as 'churned' or 'stayed'. What type of learning is this?
options: Unsupervised, because it groups customers without labels
Supervised, because the data already has the label to predict
Reinforcement, because it receives rewards for each hit
None, because prediction does not use machine learning

questions.statement: A team has a large set of articles with no categories and wants the system to discover groups of similar topics on its own. Which approach applies?
options: Supervised learning, which requires labels defined beforehand
Programming fixed rules for each possible topic
Unsupervised learning, which finds groups without labels
Reinforcement learning, which depends on a reward system

questions.statement: Which scenario characterizes reinforcement learning?
options: A query returning ready records from a database
A model trained once with examples labeled in advance
An agent that acts, receives rewards, and adjusts strategy over time
An algorithm that only groups similar data, using no labels

questions.statement: A routing system learns by testing actions and receiving a positive score when the route is fast; another team groups similar orders with no ready categories. Which types of learning appear, in order?
options: Supervised and reinforcement
Unsupervised and supervised
Reinforcement and supervised
Reinforcement and unsupervised

questions.statement: A team has transactions labeled as fraud or legitimate, but first wants to discover behavior subgroups within the frauds, with no predefined categories. Which combination makes sense?
options: Clustering the frauds and then a supervised model with the labels
Swapping the labels for rewards to apply reinforcement learning
Only supervised, because the existence of labels prevents clustering
Only reinforcement learning, because a reward is involved in the process

lessons.title: Classification, regression and clustering

blocks.value:
## The output type defines the problem type
Beyond how the model learns, the exam asks what kind of problem it solves. The clue is always what you want in the output.

**Classification** predicts a discrete category: spam or not spam, fraud or legitimate, approved or rejected. The classes are known in advance.

**Regression** predicts a continuous numeric value: a property's price, tomorrow's temperature, next week's demand.

**Clustering** (grouping) predicts nothing given in advance: it discovers natural groups in the data. It is the most-tested unsupervised technique.
Output is a known category, it is classification; output is a continuous number, it is regression; finding groups without labels, it is clustering.

## When ML is not the answer
A subtle point the exam loves: not every problem calls for machine learning. If the rules are fixed, deterministic, and well defined (computing a tax by law, applying a table discount), the right move is to program the logic, not train a model. Machine learning is worth it when patterns are complex, change over time, or are hard to describe in explicit rules.

questions.statement: A store wants to predict how many units of a product it will sell next week (a number). What type of ML problem is this?
options: Clustering, because it groups similar products
Regression, because the output is a continuous numeric value
Reinforcement, because it learns by reward and punishment
Classification, because the output is a discrete category

questions.statement: Deciding whether an incoming email is 'spam' or 'not spam' is an example of which type of problem?
options: Dimensionality reduction, because it summarizes variables
Classification, because it predicts a known category
Clustering, because it discovers groups without labels
Regression, because it predicts a continuous number

questions.statement: In which situation is using machine learning the LEAST appropriate choice?
options: Recommending content based on user behavior
Computing a tax using fixed, deterministic rules from law
Predicting product demand from historical patterns
Classifying customer reviews as positive or negative

questions.statement: A bank wants to estimate the likely loss amount in reais for each loan and also mark each customer as solvent or delinquent. What types of problem are these, in order?
options: Regression and classification
Clustering and classification
Regression and clustering
Classification and regression

questions.statement: Which scenario justifies programming explicit rules instead of training a machine learning model?
options: Patterns change every week according to user behavior
The rules are hard to describe and full of subtle exceptions
The volume of labeled examples available grows every day
The calculation follows a fixed, fully deterministic legal table

lessons.title: The ML lifecycle and the importance of data

blocks.value:
## From problem to model in production
A machine learning project follows a cycle the AIF-C01 expects you to recognize at a high level:

1. **Frame the problem**: define what you want to predict and how success will be measured.
2. **Collect and prepare the data**: gather, clean, and transform data; create variables (features).
3. **Train the model**: the algorithm adjusts its parameters from the training data.
4. **Evaluate**: measure performance on data the model has not seen in training.
5. **Deploy**: put the model to serve predictions (inference) in production.
6. **Monitor**: track quality over time and retrain when necessary.

## Essential vocabulary
A **feature (attribute)** is each input variable used to predict, like a property's area and location. A **label** is the answer you want to predict, like the price. **Training** is fitting the parameters with data; **inference** is using the already-trained model to predict on new data.

Keep the difference between training and inference: training happens once (or periodically) and is costly; inference happens all the time in production, on every requested prediction.
Bad data produces bad models. Neither a bigger model nor more data compensates for wrong or biased information: data quality is decisive.

questions.statement: In supervised ML vocabulary, what is a 'label'?
options: The internal parameter adjusted during training
Each input variable used to make the prediction
The metric that evaluates the model on the test set
The answer you want to predict, associated with each example

questions.statement: Using an already-trained model to generate predictions on new data in production is called:
options: Data collection
Training
Inference
Labeling

questions.statement: A team had a weak-performing model and discovered many wrong and missing values in the training set. Which principle does this reinforce?
options: Data quality strongly influences model quality
A bigger model automatically compensates for bad data
Test data matters more than training data
The chosen algorithm does not affect the result with lots of data

questions.statement: Put the ML lifecycle stages in the correct order: evaluate, train, prepare the data, and deploy.
options: Train, evaluate, prepare the data, and deploy
Train, prepare the data, deploy, and evaluate
Prepare the data, train, evaluate, and deploy
Prepare the data, evaluate, train, and deploy

questions.statement: About the difference between training and inference, which statement is correct?
options: Inference is the stage that adjusts model parameters on each new prediction requested in production
Training adjusts parameters and is costly; inference serves each prediction in production
Training happens continuously in production and inference runs only once
Training and inference are the same process run on different machines

lessons.title: Evaluating models: accuracy, precision, recall and overfitting

blocks.value:
## Metrics to know whether the model is good
Evaluating means comparing the model's predictions with the real answers on data it has not seen in training. For classification, a few metrics show up on the exam:

**Accuracy** is the fraction of correct predictions out of the total. Simple, but misleading when classes are imbalanced.

**Precision** answers: of the cases the model marked positive, how many really were positive? High precision means few false positives.

**Recall (sensitivity)** answers: of the cases that were truly positive, how many did the model capture? High recall means few false negatives.

## Precision vs recall: the trade-off
Which to prioritize depends on the cost of the error. In medical screening, letting a sick patient slip through (false negative) is serious, so recall is prioritized. In a filter that blocks emails, marking a legitimate email as spam (false positive) annoys the user, so precision weighs more. Rarely do you maximize both at once.

## Overfitting and underfitting
**Overfitting** happens when the model does very well on training and poorly on new data: it memorized instead of generalizing. The signature is high training accuracy and low test accuracy. **Underfitting** is the opposite: the model is too simple and does poorly on both sets. The goal is the middle ground, a model that generalizes to data it has never seen.
Did well on training and poorly on the test? Overfitting. Did poorly on both? Underfitting.

questions.statement: A model has 99% accuracy on training and 60% on the test. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Lack of data, because the model did not learn in training
Overfitting: the model memorized the training data and does not generalize
The model is perfect and ready for production
Underfitting: the model is too simple for the data

questions.statement: A medical screening must avoid at all costs classifying a sick patient as healthy. Which metric should be prioritized?
options: Model size, to fit in memory
Recall, to reduce false negatives
Training time, to speed up the model
Precision, to reduce false positives

questions.statement: Why can accuracy mislead on a very imbalanced dataset?
options: Imbalanced data increases accuracy proportionally and fairly
Always predicting the majority class gives high accuracy without predicting the rare one
Accuracy is impossible to calculate when there is imbalance
Accuracy always equals recall in those cases

questions.statement: In a filter that blocks suspicious emails, the biggest annoyance is blocking a legitimate message. Which metric should weigh more in evaluation?
options: Overall accuracy, which sums the hits of both classes
Recall, to reduce false negatives
Precision, to reduce false positives
The rate of emails processed per second

questions.statement: A model performs poorly on both the training set and the test set. What is the diagnosis and a coherent action?
options: Imbalanced classes; look only at accuracy from now on
Data leakage; reshuffle the test set again
Overfitting; immediately reduce model complexity
Underfitting; use a more expressive model or better features

lessons.title: AWS AI and ML services

blocks.value:
## Three layers of services
AWS organizes AI in layers, and recognizing the right layer for each scenario is one of the most-tested topics in the AIF-C01.

**Pre-trained AI services** deliver ready capabilities via API, with no training involved. You call and use. Examples: Amazon Rekognition (images and video), Amazon Transcribe (speech to text), Amazon Polly (text to speech), Amazon Translate (translation), Amazon Comprehend (text analysis and PII), Amazon Textract (document extraction), and Amazon Lex (chatbots).

**Amazon SageMaker** is the platform for those who want to build, train, and deploy their own models, with full control. It includes SageMaker Canvas (visual, no-code ML) for business users.

**Generative AI services**, like Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Q, are covered in the next modules.

[["I need to...","AWS service"],["Transcribe audio into text","Amazon Transcribe"],["Convert text into speech","Amazon Polly"],["Analyze images and videos","Amazon Rekognition"],["Extract sentiment and entities from text","Amazon Comprehend"],["Read fields from documents and forms","Amazon Textract"],["Translate between languages","Amazon Translate"],["Build a chatbot","Amazon Lex"],["Train a custom model","Amazon SageMaker"],["Create ML without writing code","Amazon SageMaker Canvas"]]

## Pre-trained or build from scratch?

The rule of thumb: if a ready service already solves it (transcribe, translate, analyze text), use it; it is faster and cheaper. Move to SageMaker only when you need a custom model for a company-specific problem, with your own data and control over the algorithm.

questions.statement: A startup needs to transcribe meeting audio into text quickly, training no model. Which service?
options: Amazon Comprehend, which analyzes sentiment in written text
Amazon Transcribe, a ready speech-to-text service
Amazon Polly, which generates speech from text
Amazon SageMaker, training a custom model

questions.statement: A business analyst with no coding experience wants to create ML models through a visual interface. Which tool is most suitable?
options: Amazon Athena, for SQL queries on S3
Amazon EMR, a big data platform with Spark
AWS Lambda, for running functions on demand
Amazon SageMaker Canvas, which offers no-code ML

questions.statement: A company wants to automatically extract the amount and due date from thousands of PDF invoices. Which service is most suitable?
options: Amazon Translate, which translates between languages
Amazon Textract, which extracts text and fields from documents
Amazon Polly, which converts text to speech
Amazon Rekognition, focused on image and video analysis

questions.statement: A call center wants to convert text articles into natural-sounding audio for an accessibility service, training no model. Which service solves it?
options: Amazon Transcribe, which converts speech to text
Amazon Comprehend, which analyzes sentiment
Amazon SageMaker, which trains custom models
Amazon Polly, which converts text to speech

questions.statement: A team wants to detect entities and personal data (PII) in thousands of text tickets and, separately, train a proprietary risk model with internal data. Which pair of services fits, in order?
options: Amazon Comprehend and Amazon SageMaker

modules.title: Module 2 - Generative AI and foundation models

lessons.title: What generative AI and foundation models are

blocks.value:
## From prediction to creation
Traditional machine learning predicts or classifies: given an email, is it spam or not? **Generative AI** does something different: it creates new, original content, like text, image, code, or audio, from an instruction in natural language.

The engine behind this is the **foundation model**: a large model, pre-trained on huge volumes of data, that serves as the base for many different tasks. Instead of training one model per task, you start from an already-ready foundation model and adapt it.

## What makes a foundation model special
Two characteristics define a foundation model:

**Scale and pre-training**: it learned general patterns from a massive amount of data, giving it broad knowledge without having been trained for one specific task.

**Adaptability**: the same model can summarize, translate, answer questions, write code, and classify, depending on how you instruct it. A **large language model (LLM)** is a foundation model specialized in language.
A foundation model is large, pre-trained on vast data, and adaptable to many tasks. It is not a single-task model nor a database.

questions.statement: What best characterizes a foundation model?
options: A small model trained from scratch for one specific task
A deterministic rule that does not depend on data
A vector database that stores embeddings
A large, pre-trained model that serves as the base for many tasks

questions.statement: Which task is a typical generative AI use case?
options: Summing a spreadsheet column with exact precision
Routing network packets between subnets
Applying access permission policies
Generating a draft text from an instruction

questions.statement: A large language model (LLM) is best described as:
options: A foundation model specialized in language
A translation service based on manual rules
A relational database optimized for text
A clustering algorithm for grouping documents

questions.statement: A team wants to use a single model to summarize contracts, answer questions, and draft emails. Which characteristic of foundation models makes this possible?
options: The guarantee of an identical answer for the same submitted instruction
Per-task training, redone from scratch for each new use case
The bank of ready answers embedded during pre-training
Adaptability: the same pre-trained model serves different tasks

questions.statement: Which option describes something a foundation model is NOT?
options: An adaptable base for different tasks depending on the instruction given
A model pre-trained on enormous volumes of data
The kind of model that powers language LLMs
A database returning exact excerpts from the training material

lessons.title: How an LLM works: tokens, embeddings and the context window

blocks.value:
## Tokens: the unit the model processes
An LLM does not read letters or whole words directly; it processes **tokens**, units of text that can be a word or part of one. A sentence becomes a sequence of tokens, and the model predicts the next token at each step. Cost and usage limits are usually measured in tokens, so keep the concept clear.

## Embeddings: meaning turned into numbers
To compare texts by meaning, each passage is converted into an **embedding**: a numeric representation in vector form that captures the content's sense. Texts with similar meaning end up close in that vector space. Embeddings are the foundation of semantic search and RAG, which we will see in the next module.

## Context window: how much the model sees
The **context window** is the maximum number of tokens the model considers at once, adding input and output. If the conversation or document exceeds the window, the excess must be summarized or retrieved on demand. Larger windows allow processing more text per interaction, usually at a higher cost.
A token is the unit of text processed; an embedding is meaning in vector form; the context window is the token limit per interaction.

questions.statement: In the context of an LLM, what is a token?
options: An internal parameter the model adjusts during training
A log record generated on each request to the model
A security credential authorizing access to the API
A unit of text (word or part of one) the model processes

questions.statement: What is the role of an embedding?
options: Encrypting the document before storing it
Representing a text's meaning as a numeric vector
Generating a short natural-language summary of the text
Indexing keywords in a relational database

questions.statement: What does an LLM's 'context window' represent?
options: The time the answer stays in cache
The maximum number of tokens the model considers in an interaction
The cloud region where the model runs
The maximum number of simultaneous users allowed in the service

questions.statement: A long conversation passed the limit the model considers at once, and the answers stopped reflecting the start of the dialogue. Which concept explains the problem?
options: The temperature, which discards the oldest messages in the dialogue
The token, which changes size depending on the conversation's language
The embedding, which compresses text into too small a vector
The context window, which limits the combined input and output tokens

questions.statement: A search needs to find documents with meaning similar to the question, even without shared words. Which mechanism enables that?
options: Increasing the context window until all documents fit
Reducing the per-token cost charged on the inference call
Counting how many identical tokens the texts share
Comparing embeddings: nearby vectors indicate similar meanings

lessons.title: Amazon Bedrock: foundation models via API

blocks.value:
## A single access point to several models
**Amazon Bedrock** is the AWS service for generative AI. It gives access to foundation models from several providers through a single fully managed API. You pick the model, send a prompt, and receive the answer, with no servers to provision or GPUs to manage.

Being **serverless**, Bedrock leaves the infrastructure to AWS. That lets a small team quickly experiment with and compare models, and take a generative application to production without operating the heavy part.

[["I want to...","How Bedrock helps"],["Use several foundation models","One API for models from different providers"],["Not manage servers","Serverless service, infrastructure managed by AWS"],["Ground answers in my data","Knowledge Bases (managed RAG)"],["Run multi-step tasks","Agents (action orchestration)"],["Filter unwanted content","Guardrails"],["Compare model quality","Model evaluation"]]

## What Bedrock does NOT require
A point the exam reinforces: with Bedrock you do not need to download model weights, do not need to maintain your own GPU cluster, and do not need to train anything from scratch to start. The focus is consuming models via API and, when necessary, customizing them with managed features.

questions.statement: Which service allows accessing foundation models from several providers through a single managed API, with no infrastructure to administer?
options: AWS Glue
Amazon Bedrock
Amazon S3
Amazon EC2, for compute

questions.statement: A small team wants to test several foundation models without provisioning GPUs. Which Bedrock characteristic helps?
options: It requires a dedicated GPU cluster per model tested
It is serverless: AWS manages the models' infrastructure
It only works with models trained from scratch by the team
It requires downloading the weights and hosting them yourself

questions.statement: To use Amazon Bedrock in a basic generative application, what is NOT necessary?
options: Choosing one of the foundation models available in the service
Maintaining your own GPU cluster to host the models
Having adequate permissions to access the service
Sending a prompt to the model via the API

questions.statement: A team wants to compare the quality of two foundation models and also filter unwanted content in the answers, all within Bedrock. Which features to use, in order?
options: Model evaluation and Guardrails
Agents and model evaluation
Guardrails and Knowledge Bases
Knowledge Bases and Agents

options: Writing the prompts the client application sends to the model
Defining the business rules of the generative application the client operates
Provisioning and operating the infrastructure hosting the foundation models
Choosing which model each client application should use

lessons.title: Use cases, benefits and challenges of generative AI

blocks.value:
## Where generative AI shines
Good use cases involve creating or transforming content in natural language: drafting text, summarizing long documents, answering questions, writing and explaining code, translating with nuance, and creating images from descriptions. The common point is handling open, unstructured content.

## Advantages over training from scratch
Using foundation models saves time and data: you leverage an already pre-trained model and adapt it to many tasks with little effort, instead of collecting data and training one model per problem. This speeds up prototypes and lowers the barrier to entry.

## Challenges the exam tests
Generative AI also brings challenges that need controls:

- **Variable and inaccurate responses**: the same question can produce different answers, and some may contain errors. This demands verification.
- **Hallucinations**: the model can invent plausible but false information.
- **Cost and latency**: larger models cost more and take longer.
- **Content safety**: without controls, the model can generate unwanted content.

What generative AI should NOT do: exact calculations, deterministic rules, or operations requiring perfect reproducibility. For those, use traditional logic.
Open content (text, code, image, summary) fits generative AI; exact calculation and fixed rules fit traditional logic.

questions.statement: What is a central advantage of using foundation models instead of training from scratch?
options: They guarantee zero inference cost at any volume
They eliminate any risk of generating incorrect answers on tasks
They come pre-trained and adapt to several tasks with little effort
They dispense with using any data in new cases

questions.statement: What is a known challenge when adopting generative AI in production?
options: The models only work offline, with no API access
They cannot process more than one language at a time
The answers may vary and contain inaccuracies, requiring verification
It is impossible to restrict the topics the model answers about

questions.statement: For which task is generative AI LEAST suitable?
options: Drafting a customer support reply
Computing taxes using fixed and exact tax rules
Explaining a piece of code in plain language
Summarizing a long report into a few paragraphs

questions.statement: Which set of tasks aligns with generative AI's strengths?
options: Applying table discounts defined in a closed contract
Summarizing documents, drafting text, and explaining code snippets
Summing invoices guaranteeing perfect reproducibility
Computing payroll with fixed rules and exact results

questions.statement: A director proposes replacing the company's tax calculation with an LLM to modernize the system. What is the technically correct objection?
options: Exact, deterministic calculation calls for traditional logic, not generation
You only need to increase the context window until the legislation fits
LLMs cannot process numbers under any circumstance
The idea works, as long as the temperature is set to zero

lessons.title: Amazon Q and managed generative assistants

blocks.value:
## Assistants ready for work
Besides Bedrock (the platform for building), AWS offers ready generative assistants under the **Amazon Q** brand.

**Amazon Q Business** is an assistant that answers employees' questions based on the company's internal data (documents, wikis, systems), respecting each person's permissions. It is the option when the goal is giving answers grounded in corporate knowledge.

**Amazon Q Developer** helps technology teams with code generation and explanation and support for development tasks on AWS.

## How to choose in the scenario
If the statement asks for an assistant that answers from internal documents and respects access, think **Amazon Q Business**. If it asks to build a custom generative application, with model choice and own integration, think **Amazon Bedrock**. Services like Rekognition (images), Athena (SQL queries), and Polly (voice) are not corporate generative assistants.

options: Amazon Polly

options: Amazon Comprehend, for pre-trained text analysis
Amazon Translate, for translation between languages
Amazon Bedrock, the platform for building with foundation models
Amazon Q Business, a ready assistant for internal company use

questions.statement: Which service supports development teams with code generation and explanation on AWS?
options: Amazon Q Developer
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon Macie

lessons.title: Hallucinations and the limits of generative AI

blocks.value:
## When the model makes things up
A **hallucination** occurs when the model generates plausible but false information: a nonexistent citation, an invented fact, a reference with fabricated authors and dates. The model does not lie on purpose; it predicts the most likely text, and sometimes the most likely is not true.

That is why generative AI outputs in precision-demanding contexts need verification. Do not confuse hallucination with bias (which comes from imbalance in the data) or with overfitting (which is about generalization in traditional ML).

## How to reduce the risk
Some practices help mitigate hallucinations and limits:

- **Ground answers in trusted data** (RAG), instead of trusting only the model's memory.
- **Apply guardrails** to block unwanted content.
- **Keep human review** on high-impact decisions.
- **Ask the model to cite sources** when possible.

These topics appear in detail in the applications and responsible AI modules.
Hallucination is plausible but false content. Powerful generative AI still requires verification, guardrails, and human supervision.

questions.statement: An LLM answered citing an article that does not exist, with invented authors. What is this behavior called?
options: Bias, when the model reflects imbalance present in the data
Overfitting, when the model memorizes the training data
Hallucination, when the model generates something plausible but false
Latency, when the model takes long to answer

questions.statement: Which practice helps reduce hallucinations in a generative application?
options: Grounding answers in retrieved trusted data (RAG)
Increasing the temperature to get more creative answers
Removing all verification to speed up answers
Turning off any content guardrails

questions.statement: Why do generative AI outputs require verification in precision-demanding contexts?
options: The model predicts the most likely text, which is not always true
The answers are identical on every run, with no variation
Verification eliminates the model's inference cost
The model always refuses to answer factual questions

questions.statement: According to the lesson, which pair of concepts should NOT be confused with hallucination?
options: Data bias and overfitting
Plausible yet incorrect information
A false reference with nonexistent authors
An invented citation and fabricated data

questions.statement: Besides grounding answers with RAG, which controls does the lesson recommend for living with generative AI's limits?
options: Disabling human verification to speed up the workflow
Guardrails, human review on impactful decisions, and citing sources
Trusting the model's memory instead of retrieved data
Increasing the temperature to diversify the generated answers

lessons.title: Prompt engineering: zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought

blocks.value:
## The instruction shapes the answer
**Prompt engineering** is the practice of structuring the instruction to get better answers from an LLM, without changing the model. It is the fastest and cheapest way to improve results: you change the text you send, not the model's weights.

A good prompt usually makes the task, the expected answer format, the tone, and any constraints clear. Small wording changes can have a big effect on output quality.

## Three techniques that show up on the exam
**Zero-shot**: you ask for the task without giving examples. E.g., "Classify the sentiment of this sentence". Works well on common tasks.

**Few-shot**: you include a few examples of input and desired output inside the prompt itself, to guide the format and style. Also called in-context learning, because the model learns from the examples right there, with no training.

**Chain-of-thought**: you ask the model to explain the step-by-step reasoning before giving the final answer. This usually improves logic and calculation tasks.

[["Technique","What it is","Good for"],["Zero-shot","Asks for the task with no examples","Common, direct tasks"],["Few-shot","Includes a few examples in the prompt","Fixing the output's format and style"],["Chain-of-thought","Asks for step-by-step reasoning","Logic and calculation problems"]]

Structuring instructions to get better answers from an LLM
Configuring the VPC network where the model runs

options: Fine-tuning, which readjusts the model's internal weights

RAG, which retrieves external documents

questions.statement: Asking the model to explain its reasoning step by step before the final answer is the technique of:
options: Quantizing the model's weights

lessons.title: Inference parameters: temperature, top-p and max tokens

blocks.value:
## Controlling the answer's behavior
When calling an LLM, besides the prompt you adjust inference parameters that change the output's style, without changing the model.

**Temperature** controls randomness. Low temperature makes answers more predictable and focused; high temperature makes them more varied and creative. For factual tasks, prefer low temperature; for brainstorming, higher.

**Top-p (nucleus sampling)** limits the choice to the most likely words that add up to a certain probability. Together with temperature, it governs how diverse the answer is.

## Max tokens and what it does NOT do
**Max tokens** limits the answer's size: when the ceiling is reached, generation stops. It is useful for controlling cost and avoiding overly long answers.

Watch out for traps: max tokens does not increase creativity (that is temperature/top-p), does not guarantee the answer is correct, and does not define how many times you can call the API (those are the service's quotas).
Temperature and top-p control the answer's diversity; max tokens controls the size. None of them guarantees the answer is true.

options: Using high temperature, for more varied answers

options: Reducing the maximum tokens allowed in the answer

lessons.title: RAG: grounding answers in trusted data

blocks.value:
## The problem RAG solves
A foundation model only knows what was in its pre-training data; it does not know your company's internal documents or information that changed afterwards. Asking it to answer about those invites hallucinations.

**Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)** solves this: before answering, the system retrieves relevant passages from an external database and includes them in the prompt, grounding the answer in real, specific information. The model is not changed; what changes is the context it receives.

## The role of the vector database
To retrieve by meaning, documents are converted into embeddings and stored in a **vector database**. At question time, the question also becomes an embedding, and the database returns the most similar passages, which go into the prompt. That way the search is semantic, not just keyword-based.

Benefits of RAG: it reduces hallucinations, uses updated data without retraining, and allows citing sources, increasing trust.
RAG retrieves external data and injects it into the prompt. It reduces hallucinations, uses current data without retraining, and allows citing sources.

questions.statement: What is Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)?
options: Compressing the model to fit in little memory

options: Increasing the temperature for more creative answers

questions.statement: What is the role of a vector database in a RAG solution?
options: Storing embeddings and retrieving the most similar passages

questions.statement: In a RAG flow, what is the correct sequence when receiving a user question?
options: Retrain the model with the received question and only then answer the user

options: Cheaper model, smaller weights, and always-reduced latency

Eliminating the need to maintain any vector database

lessons.title: Knowledge Bases and Agents for Amazon Bedrock

blocks.value:
## Managed RAG with Knowledge Bases
Building RAG from scratch involves generating embeddings, maintaining a vector database, and orchestrating retrieval. **Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock** handles that in a managed way: you point to your data sources and the service handles ingestion, embeddings, and retrieval, connecting the foundation model to your documents.

## Multi-step actions with Agents
Sometimes answering is not enough; you need to act. **Agents for Amazon Bedrock** lets a foundation model run multi-step tasks, calling APIs and systems to complete a request. An agent can, for example, check stock, create an order, and confirm the deadline, orchestrating the necessary calls.

Do not confuse Bedrock features: Knowledge Bases is for RAG; Agents is for orchestrating actions; Guardrails is for filtering content; model evaluation is for comparing models.

lessons.title: Fine-tuning, RAG or prompt: how to choose

blocks.value:
## Three ways to adapt a model
When a ready foundation model is not enough, there are three paths, from lightest to heaviest:

**Prompt engineering**: change only the instruction. Fast, cheap, no model changes. Always start here.

**RAG**: give the model access to external data at answer time. Ideal when the information is company-specific or changes often, since you just update the database, with no retraining.

**Fine-tuning**: continue the model's training with your own data, adjusting the weights to specialize it in a task or style. It is more costly, and the knowledge gets fixed in the weights.

## The question that decides
If the information changes every week, RAG usually beats fine-tuning: you update the database and done, without retraining the model on every change. Fine-tuning shines when you want to specialize the model's behavior or style in a stable way, not when the content is volatile.

A good rule of thumb: prompt to adjust the instruction, RAG to bring in current and specific knowledge, fine-tuning to specialize behavior.

[["Approach","Changes the weights?","Best when"],["Prompt engineering","No","Adjusting instruction and format quickly"],["RAG","No","Using specific or ever-changing data"],["Fine-tuning","Yes","Specializing behavior or style in a stable way"]]
Ever-changing data calls for RAG (update the database, no retraining). Specializing behavior calls for fine-tuning.

lessons.title: Model choice and prompt security

blocks.value:
## The biggest model is not always the right one
Foundation models vary in size, cost, latency, and capability. Smaller models tend to cost less and answer faster, with less capability; larger ones solve more complex tasks, but cost more and take longer. The choice balances these factors for the use case.

For a high-volume chatbot with simple answers, a smaller model may be ideal. For complex reasoning, a larger model is worth it. Testing and comparing (with Bedrock's model evaluation) helps decide with data.

## Prompt injection: an LLM-specific risk
When an LLM receives user input, **prompt injection** arises: a malicious input that tries to subvert the system's original instructions, making the model ignore the rules and follow the attacker's. It is a risk specific to LLM applications, different from generic infrastructure problems.

Mitigations include guardrails, clearly separating instructions from user data, and validating outputs. Content safety details appear in the responsible AI module.
Smaller model: cheaper and faster, less capable. Prompt injection: input that tries to subvert the system's instructions.

questions.statement: When choosing a foundation model for a high-volume, low-cost chatbot, which trade-off to consider?
options: Larger models are always cheaper and faster than smaller ones

Smaller models always beat larger ones on any task

lessons.title: What responsible AI is and its dimensions

blocks.value:
## Building AI with responsibility
**Responsible AI** is the set of principles and practices for developing and using AI systems in a fair, safe, transparent, and trustworthy way. It is not an optional feature: it is a dimension that cuts across the whole lifecycle, from data to monitoring.

The AIF-C01 expects you to recognize the core dimensions and associate each one with AWS practices and services.

[["Dimension","What it means"],["Fairness","Treating different groups equitably"],["Explainability","Understanding why the model decided"],["Transparency","Making clear how the system works and its limits"],["Robustness and safety","Working reliably and avoiding harm"],["Privacy","Protecting people's data"],["Governance","Defining responsibilities, controls, and oversight"]]

## Why this shows up on the exam
AI solutions affect people: credit, hiring, health, content moderation. Without care, they can reproduce injustices, make unexplainable decisions, or generate harmful content. Recognizing that fairness, explainability, transparency, safety, and privacy are pillars (and not "increase parameters" or "hide how it works") is what the exam wants.

lessons.title: Bias and fairness in AI models

blocks.value:
## What bias is
**Bias** in AI is a systematic error that unfairly favors or harms certain groups. It usually comes from the data: if the history used in training is already imbalanced, the model learns and reproduces (or even amplifies) that imbalance.

A classic example: a recruiting model trained on biased past hires starts favoring the same profile, perpetuating the injustice. The problem is not the algorithm inventing; it is learning the bias already present in the data.

## Detect and reduce with SageMaker Clarify
**Amazon SageMaker Clarify** helps detect bias in data and in the model and explain predictions. It measures, for example, whether a group is under-represented or receives systematically different outcomes, helping the team identify and mitigate the problem before and after training.

Reducing bias involves more representative data, checking with fairness metrics, and often human oversight on sensitive decisions.
Bias is a systematic error that treats groups unfairly, often inherited from imbalanced data. SageMaker Clarify helps detect it.

lessons.title: Explainability, transparency and documentation

blocks.value:
## Explaining decisions
**Explainability** is the ability to understand why a model made a given decision. In sensitive applications, like granting credit, it is essential: it lets you justify the decision to those affected and meet regulatory requirements. Explaining does not eliminate errors or speed up training; it gives visibility into the model's reasoning.

## Document to govern
Two transparency tools show up on the exam:

**Model cards** document, for each model, the purpose, the data used, the metrics, and the known limitations. They serve governance and let model users know what to expect.

**AWS AI Service Cards** are documents published by AWS describing intended use cases, limitations, and design choices of its AI services, promoting responsible use and transparency.

lessons.title: Content safety and human oversight

blocks.value:
## Guardrails: content barriers
In generative applications, toxic, dangerous, or out-of-scope answers must be prevented. **Amazon Bedrock Guardrails** apply content filters, block denied topics, and help protect sensitive data in answers. It is the managed way to keep the assistant within the limits set by the company, a safety and harm-mitigation measure.

## Keeping the human in the loop
On high-impact decisions, keeping **human review (human in the loop)** is a central responsible AI safeguard: a person reviews or approves the model's decisions, preventing serious errors from going straight through. Removing supervision to "gain speed", hiding decisions from those affected, or raising the model's creativity go in the opposite direction of responsible use.

Together, guardrails (limiting content) and human oversight (reviewing decisions) reduce the main risks of operating AI in production.
Guardrails limit the generated content; human oversight reviews high-impact decisions. Both are pillars of responsible AI.

lessons.title: Shared responsibility and access control

blocks.value:
## Who takes care of what
In the cloud, security is a **shared responsibility**. AWS takes care of security **of** the cloud: physical infrastructure, hardware, network, and the operation of managed services. The customer takes care of security **in** the cloud: who accesses what, how data is configured and used, and the application's permissions.

In a managed AI service, this means AWS maintains the platform and patches, while you define access control and governance of your input and output data.

## Least privilege with IAM
Access control on AWS is done with **AWS IAM (Identity and Access Management)**. The best practice is the **principle of least privilege**: grant only the strictly necessary permissions to each user or service, and nothing more. This reduces the attack surface.

Insecure practices the exam rejects: giving administrator permission to everyone, sharing the root account key, or disabling authentication to "make it easier".
AWS takes care of security of the cloud; the customer takes care of security in the cloud, including access and data. Use IAM with least privilege.

lessons.title: Data protection: encryption, Macie and PII

blocks.value:
## Encrypt at rest and in transit
Protecting an AI solution's data starts with **encryption**: at rest (stored data) and in transit (data traveling the network). **AWS KMS (Key Management Service)** manages the encryption keys. Keeping data in plain text, in open buckets, or without logs weakens security and is the opposite of recommended.

## Discovering and protecting sensitive data
Personal data (PII) and other sensitive data must be identified and protected. **Amazon Macie** uses machine learning to discover and protect sensitive data, like PII, stored in Amazon S3. It is the typical answer when the scenario talks about finding and protecting personal data in large volumes of files.

Other services have different roles: Comprehend also detects PII in text, but Macie is the specialist in scanning S3 at scale.
Encrypt at rest and in transit (KMS). To discover and protect PII in S3 at scale, use Amazon Macie.

lessons.title: Privacy in Bedrock and private connectivity

blocks.value:
## What happens to your data in Bedrock
A common question: are the prompts and data I send to Amazon Bedrock used to train the third-party base models? Bedrock's privacy posture is that **customer data is not used to train the base foundation models** nor shared with the model providers. This gives companies confidence to use the service with their own data.

## Traffic without going through the internet
So that calls to an AI service do not travel over the public internet, keeping the traffic inside the AWS network, you use **AWS PrivateLink**. It connects your VPC to the service privately, reducing exposure. Services like Route 53 (DNS), SNS (messaging), and Cost Explorer (costs) do not have this private connectivity function.
In Bedrock, customer data does not train the base models. For private connectivity to the AWS network, use AWS PrivateLink.

Amazon Route 53, a DNS service for resolving domain names

options: It guarantees the data does not train the base models or reach the providers

It publishes all prompts in an open repository

lessons.title: Monitoring, auditing and compliance

blocks.value:
## Tracking in production
After deploying, you must monitor operation and quality over time. **Amazon CloudWatch** tracks operational metrics and logs (latency, errors, usage). **Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor** detects drift in model quality, warning when performance drops and retraining is worth it.

## Auditing and proving compliance
For governance, two services appear:

**AWS CloudTrail** records the API calls made in the account, allowing you to audit who did what and when, a common compliance requirement.

**AWS Artifact** is the portal with AWS's compliance reports and certifications (ISO, SOC, and others), useful in audits.

**Data governance** completes the picture: tracking the origin and transformations of data (lineage) supports audit, compliance, and reproducibility, showing where the data came from and how it was handled.

blocks.value:
## What you covered
You covered the five AIF-C01 domains:

- **AI and ML fundamentals**: the AI, ML, and deep learning hierarchy; types of learning; classification, regression, and clustering; the lifecycle; metrics; and the AWS AI and ML services.
- **Generative AI and foundation models**: what they are, tokens, embeddings, the context window, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Q, and hallucinations.
- **Applying foundation models**: prompt engineering, inference parameters, RAG, Knowledge Bases and Agents, and the choice between prompt, RAG, and fine-tuning.
- **Responsible AI**: fairness, bias, explainability, transparency, guardrails, and human oversight.
- **Security, compliance and governance**: shared responsibility, IAM, encryption, Macie, Bedrock privacy, PrivateLink, monitoring, auditing, and compliance.

## How to reinforce
When reviewing, train two reflexes the exam demands: associating a scenario with the right AWS service (for example, "find PII in S3" leads to Macie; "connect the model to my data" leads to Knowledge Bases) and distinguishing close concepts (generative vs agentic, RAG vs fine-tuning, precision vs recall, bias vs hallucination).

The best thermometer is practicing with exam-format questions, reviewing each explanation. Take the AWS AI Practitioner practice exam in the Practice Exams tab to measure where you stand and reinforce weak points.
Two exam reflexes: connect the scenario to the right service and separate similar concepts. Practice with the practice exam and review the explanations.
